doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Wilbur Harden, Cedar Walton's foot, and Clarence Shaw
summary: Fuller says he could hear Wilbur Harden thinking while playing, couldn't watch Cedar Walton's foot, and describes Clarence Shaw's unpredictable lines.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, he and Wilbur Harden. Now, Wilbur, ‘Trane loved him, but I couldn’t stand to watch him. He’s a guy that you, literally, could hear him think. He would stand on the bandstand and be moving about “click, click, click, click” He would say, (scats very sparse, calculated melody).

He’s editing as he’s trying to play. I mean, do you know what that is to watch? Win, and Cedar I couldn’t stand to watch. Cedar had a way like Elvin. Cedar’s time movement with his foot, I couldn’t look at it
Because he would throw you off?
He would throw me off because his foot would move out of rhythm, with no distinct pattern or nothing. Sometimes, I would stand there and look like, “What the hell! How did you come up with that one?”
But, Wilbur Harden, on top of his playing was his significance in writing
Yeah, some writing but not a whole lot. Then, there was another guy that was just like him. ‘Trane didn’t like him too much. He ended up with Mingus. Clarence something…

Yeah, you know all these guys. Yeah, he was just late Wilbur. I never could get the gist of his… It was always something that was… He kept anticipating that he was going to play something but it would always be the complete opposite of what you thought he would do. The line would be so discombobulated. You would be like, “Where did that come from?” That’s the way he heard it so you can question the guy. I used to stand next to him and say, “Nobody’s home.”
